title: Differential Diagnosis Principles
subtitle: Key Differentiating Features Across Wrist & Hand Conditions

content.text: Differential diagnosis is the process of distinguishing between conditions that share similar signs and symptoms. This lesson summarises the key differentiating features across the wrist and hand conditions covered in this course.
Understanding differential diagnosis helps you identify the most likely condition and tailor your treatment approach appropriately.

items: UCL of MCP 1 — ulnar-sided thumb pain, positive UCL stress test
TFCC injury — deep ulnar wrist pain, positive ulnocarpal stress test, difficulty with weight bearing
De Quervain's — pain distal to extensor retinaculum, positive Finkelstein test
Intersection syndrome — pain proximal to extensor retinaculum
Wartenberg syndrome — paresthesia in radial nerve distribution
CMC 1 OA — pain around snuffbox, worse with radial deviation
FPL tenosynovitis — palmar thumb pain, AROM more provocative than RROM
Trigger finger — clicking/locking during extension, palpable nodule
Dupuytren's — painless, consistent stiffness, dimpling of palm
OA: morning stiffness < 1 hour, affects PIP & DIP, hypomobility, Bouchard's/Heberden's nodes
RA: morning stiffness > 2 hours, affects MCP, hypermobility possible, ulnar drift, systemic
Dupuytren: painless, consistent stiffness, dimpling of palm, affects fascia
Trigger finger: painful, clicking/clunking/locking during extension, nodule at A1 pulley

content.text: In tenosynovitis conditions (FPL, De Quervain's), AROM is generally MORE provocative than RROM because the tendon must move through the irritated sheath. If isometric testing is more provocative, consider muscle strain instead.

items: TFCC: pain with overpressure of ulnar deviation and pronation, NOT with radial deviation
Wrist UCL sprain: ulnar pain with overpressure of radial deviation
Gather a thorough history — onset, location, aggravating/easing factors
Perform ROM testing (AROM, PROM, RROM) to identify patterns
Perform relevant muscle testing
Perform applicable special tests
Assess functional abilities
Consider differentials based on findings

content.text: Accurate differential diagnosis is critical because the treatment approach differs significantly between conditions. For example:

items: Joint mobilisation is beneficial for OA but contraindicated for RA
Extrinsic hand strengthening is appropriate for OA but not RA (increases ulnar drift)
Deep pressure is avoided in tenosynovitis but may be used in some sprain treatments
Heat is beneficial for OA but should be avoided directly over inflamed tendon sheaths

content.text: Each condition has a specific clinical impression format. Key elements to include:

items: Sprain: affected ligament, severity, stage of healing
Tenosynovitis: affected tendon, severity, chronic or flared-up
Osteoarthritis: affected joint, severity
Dupuytren: duration, severity
Trigger finger: affected tendon, severity
TFCC: onset (traumatic or gradual), chronicity
Fracture: stage (pre/post consolidation), severity, summary of impairments

quiz.question: A patient presents with painless, consistent stiffness of the ring finger and dimpling of the palm. Which condition is most likely?
quiz.explanation: Dupuytren's is normally painless with consistent stiffness and dimpling of the palm. Trigger finger is typically painful with clicking/locking.

quiz.question: In tenosynovitis conditions (FPL, De Quervain's), which type of testing is generally MORE provocative?
quiz.explanation: In tenosynovitis, AROM is generally more provocative because the tendon must move through the irritated sheath during active movement.

quiz.question: Why is joint mobilisation contraindicated in RA but indicated in OA?
options: RA joints are too painful for mobilisation
RA causes hypermobility and compromised joint structures; OA causes hypomobility
OA joints have better blood supply for healing
RA is systemic so local treatment doesn't help
quiz.explanation: In OA, joints are hypomobile (mobilisation helps). In RA, the inflammatory process destroys synovial membranes and joint capsules, leading to instability and potential hypermobility (mobilisation is contraindicated).
